content: The document is a supplement to the 2014 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations, published in July 2015. It provides technical guidance to assist countries in planning and monitoring efforts to address HIV among key populations, including men who have sex with men, people in prisons and other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. The document focuses on monitoring and evaluating the implementation of a comprehensive package of interventions designed to address HIV in these populations. The framework outlined in the document is intended to help plan and assess progress at national and subnational levels. It emphasizes the involvement of government agencies, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), communities, and service providers in developing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating HIV prevention, treatment, and care programs for key populations. The framework builds on an existing WHO, UNODC, and UNAIDS technical guide for setting targets for universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, and care for people who inject drugs. The document provides countries with a set of harmonized indicators to evaluate the implementation of the comprehensive package of interventions. These indicators are aligned with those used by other United Nations (UN) and donor agencies and meet established standards. The indicators are designed to provide meaningful and practical data for policy development, effective programming, and reporting to donor organizations. Only indicators that can be practically reported at the national level and for which data are commonly available are included. In countries with more advanced data collection systems, additional indicators may be used to examine program coverage using programmatic data. The document also offers guidance on setting targets for these indicators. It recognizes that HIV epidemics among key populations vary by country and that each country is at a different stage of progress in scaling up programs. Setting clear, ambitious, but achievable targets helps plan for the scale-up of programs with the greatest possible impact. The target-setting process is most effective when it involves multisectoral collaboration and meaningful participation from key populations. The document proposes indicative targets for selected indicators to assist countries in calibrating their own targets and responses. The content of the document is derived from existing WHO guidance and integrates various aspects of programming for HIV, tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among key populations. It also references related key UN documents and reporting processes. The comprehensive package of interventions for key populations includes two main components: 1. Essential health sector interventions: Comprehensive condom and lubricant programming. Harm reduction interventions for substance use, including needle and syringe programs (NSPs), opioid substitution therapy (OST), and naloxone. Behavioral interventions. HIV testing and counseling. HIV treatment and care. Prevention and management of co-infections and other comorbidities, including viral hepatitis, TB, and mental health conditions. Sexual and reproductive health interventions, including contraception, diagnosis and treatment of STIs, and cervical screening. 2. Essential strategies for an enabling environment: Supportive legislation, policy, and financial commitment, including decriminalization of behaviors of key populations. Addressing stigma and discrimination, including in the health sector. Community empowerment. Addressing violence against people from key populations. The document emphasizes the importance of community engagement in the assessment process. Members of key populations play a critical role in program design and evaluation, highlighting strategies for improvement and developing appropriate targets. Findings from the assessment process should be shared with communities for their use. To guide program development and management, the indicators can also be used for preparing proposals or reporting progress to donor organizations. Target setting is fundamental to effective monitoring and evaluation. Targets define what a successful national program or project should achieve within a specific timeframe. They should be set for both cross-cutting and intervention-specific indicators at national and subnational levels. Modeling can help identify how different target levels will affect the epidemic. The document provides guidance on setting targets for the listed indicators and proposes indicative targets to assist countries in calibrating their own targets. The indicators require data from various sources, including desk reviews, expert consultations, and programmatic or administrative data. Data collection methods must be consistent across service providers to enable aggregation at the national level. Community participation in the assessment process is essential, and findings should be shared with communities for their use. It provides practical guidance for countries to monitor and evaluate their HIV response among key populations, ensuring that programs are accessible, effective, and aligned with national and international goals.
